items.title: The Domesday Book recorded almost every pig in England
items.claim: William I commissioned the Domesday survey in 1085, completed 1086. How detailed was it?

options.text: It listed only the major landholders and royal manors
It recorded landholders, ploughs, mills, fishponds, livestock and even individual peasants down to the level of swineherds — over 13,000 places
It was a list of military obligations only

items.reveal_title: Not one ox or cow escaped
items.reveal:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (E text) complained: 'So very narrowly did he have it investigated that there was no single hide nor a yard of land, nor indeed (it is a shame to relate but it seemed no shame to him to do) one ox nor one cow nor one pig which was left out.'

Commissioners visited every shire, took sworn testimony, and produced the survey in around a year. The original manuscripts (Great Domesday and Little Domesday) survive at The National Archives, Kew.
items.why: Medieval government is often dismissed as primitive. Domesday is more administratively detailed than anything attempted in Europe for centuries afterwards.

items.title: Edwin Chadwick's 1842 report drove the 1848 Public Health Act
items.claim: What was the immediate origin of British public health legislation?

options.text: A spontaneous parliamentary initiative without prior research

Edwin Chadwick's 'Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population' (1842) documented appalling urban conditions; the cholera epidemic of 1848-49 (around 53,000 dead in England and Wales) prompted the Public Health Act 1848 creating the General Board of Health and local boards
Disraeli's 1875 Act was the first such law
The 1848 Act applied only to Scotland

items.reveal:
Chadwick was a Poor Law commissioner and disciple of Jeremy Bentham. His report, partly self-funded, argued that disease and poverty were linked to environmental conditions — drains, water, ventilation, cesspits.

The 1848 Public Health Act was permissive: local boards could be established by petition or where mortality exceeded 23 per 1,000. The 1875 Public Health Act under Disraeli made provisions compulsory and gave local authorities effective powers over water, sewers, housing, food and nuisance.

John Simon (chief medical officer from 1855) institutionalised the role of medical officers of health across the country.
items.why: Modern state public health did not begin with the NHS. It began with sanitarian engineers and statisticians in the 1840s-70s, who treated mortality data as a political argument.

items.title: Thomas Becket was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170

options.text: Becket died of natural causes during a service

Four knights of Henry II — Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy, Richard le Breton — murdered Archbishop Becket in Canterbury Cathedral after Henry's outburst 'Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?'
He was executed for treason after a public trial

items.reveal:
Becket and Henry had clashed for years over the jurisdiction of church courts (Constitutions of Clarendon, 1164). Becket had fled to France, returned in 1170, and excommunicated bishops who had supported Henry. The king's exact words are disputed but the four knights took them as licence.

Becket was canonised in 1173. Henry II did public penance at Canterbury in 1174, walking barefoot and being scourged by monks. The shrine became one of medieval Europe's major pilgrimage sites — the setting of Chaucer's 'Canterbury Tales' (1380s).

Henry VIII destroyed the shrine in 1538 during the Dissolution.
items.why: Church-state conflict was the defining political question of high medieval Europe. Becket's murder dramatised the limits of royal power over the church — and made Canterbury a centre of European devotion for 350 years.
